records_read.citation: Aps C, Reynolds F. The effect of concentration on vasoactivity of bupivacaine and lignocaine. Br J Anaesth 1976;48(12):1171-4
records_read.what_it_matches_or_misses: Matches every element: human skin, intradermal, plain bupivacaine at three strengths plus lignocaine at three, double-blind in 31 volunteers, duration of action as an outcome. Its abstract states duration was unaffected by concentration except at the highest bupivacaine strength tested, which outlasted the other solutions. Full text subscription-only and not in Europe PMC.

records_read.citation: Cederholm I, Akerman B, Evers H. Local analgesic and vascular effects of intradermal ropivacaine and bupivacaine in various concentrations with and without addition of adrenaline in man. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 1994;38(4):322-7
records_read.what_it_matches_or_misses: Matches every element and is a second, independent test of the same question: randomised, double-blind, intradermal wheals in 10 healthy volunteers, plain bupivacaine at three strengths (plus ropivacaine at four), pin-prick dermal analgesia as the outcome. The page reports its per-strength bupivacaine medians elsewhere (equal at every strength) but does not credit it under this heading.

records_read.citation: Aps C, Reynolds F. An intradermal study of the local anaesthetic and vascular effects of the isomers of bupivacaine. Br J Clin Pharmacol 1978;6(1):63-8
records_read.what_it_matches_or_misses: The later companion by the same two authors, two years after 1976: intradermal, double-blind, 17 volunteers, eight concentrations of each bupivacaine isomer, duration of action at 50 per cent recovery. A concentration-duration study in human skin, but of the isomers rather than the racemate and over a lower concentration range, so it does not by itself settle the racemic question. A free full-text scan is held in Europe PMC as PMC1429379.

records_read.citation: Willatts DG, Reynolds F. Comparison of the vasoactivity of amide and ester local anaesthetics. An intradermal study. Br J Anaesth 1985;57(10):1006-11
records_read.what_it_matches_or_misses: Same group, same route and outcome, 10 volunteers, double-blind; reports duration concentration-dependent for all six agents studied. Misses the intervention element: bupivacaine was not among the six.

records_read.citation: Reynolds F, Bryson TH, Nicholas AD. Intradermal study of a new local anaesthetic agent aptocaine. Br J Anaesth 1976;48(4):347-54
records_read.what_it_matches_or_misses: Same group and route, 28 then 27 volunteers, double-blind; its abstract also states duration of action was unaffected by concentration. Bupivacaine appears only as a single-strength comparator, so it does not test bupivacaine across strengths.

records_read.what_it_matches_or_misses: Intradermal bupivacaine at four strengths in 10 volunteers, but the outcome is skin perfusion by laser Doppler imaging, not duration of analgesia. Misses the outcome element.

quote: Ropivacaine, a new long-acting amino-amide local anaesthetic agent, and bupivacaine, in various concentrations with or without addition of adrenaline, were tested in a randomized, double-blind study using intradermal wheals.
proposed_wording: Two human intradermal studies have timed plain bupivacaine at three strengths side by side. Aps and Reynolds 1976 (PMID 1023952), double-blind in 31 volunteers, report duration of action unaffected by concentration except at the highest strength tested, which outlasted the other solutions. Cederholm, Akerman and Evers 1994 (PMID 8067217), randomised and double-blind in 10 volunteers, report the same median duration of complete dermal analgesia at each bupivacaine strength. The same 1976 authors also published an intradermal concentration-duration study of the two bupivacaine isomers in 17 volunteers (Aps and Reynolds 1978, PMID 666948), whose full text is held free in Europe PMC as PMC1429379. The two racemic studies disagree in direction; the 1976 full text was not read here.
reason: A study matching every element the claim says is absent exists, and there are two of them rather than one. Aps and Reynolds 1976 (PMID 1023952) is human skin, intradermal, plain bupivacaine at three strengths, double-blind, with duration of action as the outcome; Cederholm 1994 (PMID 8067217) is the same design in 10 volunteers and reports equal median duration at every bupivacaine strength. So the page's 'the one study that tested three strengths' is too narrow: a second intradermal multi-strength timing exists, and it runs against the 1976 exception rather than with it. What remains genuinely unresolved is the direction, not the existence of evidence, so the correction needed is to the wording about how much evidence there is. The bupivacaine page states its negatives flatly, with no search-limited scoping convention, so the sentence is judged as written. The 1978 companion that the page quotes against the 1976 abstract is itself readable: Europe PMC holds a free scan as PMC1429379, although the fulltext XML endpoint returned HTTP 500 and the PDF could not be parsed in this session.
needs_full_text: Aps C, Reynolds F 1976, Br J Anaesth 48(12):1171-4, PMID 1023952 - full text, to reconcile the abstract's exception at the higher strength with the same authors' later description; subscription-only and not in Europe PMC.

Aps C, Reynolds F 1978, Br J Clin Pharmacol 6(1):63-8, PMID 666948 - free scanned full text exists in Europe PMC as PMC1429379; the fulltext XML endpoint returned HTTP 500 here and ebi.ac.uk is blocked by the network egress proxy, so it was not read in this session.
_note: the page reports one study that tested three strengths and the same authors' later contrary description of their own work

records_read.citation: Wehrfritz A, Namer B, Ihmsen H, et al. Differential effects on sensory functions and measures of epidermal nerve fiber density after application of a lidocaine patch on healthy human skin. Eur J Pain 2011;15(9):907-12
records_read.what_it_matches_or_misses: The one skin measurement the claim itself names, and the abstract confirms the page's description of it: randomised, double-blinded, healthy volunteers, epidermal nerve fibre density in skin blister roofs after 42 days, a moderate but significant decrease. records_read.what_it_matches_or_misses: Measures local-anaesthetic damage to nerve-supporting cells, in cultured neonatal rat Schwann cells and in rat sciatic nerve exposed through a perineural catheter. Misses the population element: neither arm is skin.

quote: A degeneration of epidermal nerve fibers has previously been demonstrated for patches containing the TRPV1-agonist capsaicin and our findings suggest that this effect might also be relevant for lidocaine patches.
proposed_wording: No study measuring nerve damage in skin after an injected local anaesthetic was found in searches of Europe PMC and in the earlier worker's PubMed searches through October 2026. The one skin measurement found is of a topical lidocaine patch, which lowered epidermal nerve fibre density in healthy volunteers after 42 days in a randomised, double-blinded study (Wehrfritz et al. 2011, PMID 21530339). For an injected substance the method has been applied, but to capsaicin rather than to an anaesthetic: intradermal capsaicin in humans produced degeneration and subsequent reinnervation of epidermal nerve fibres (PMID 9787000).
reason: Both halves of the claim hold on these searches. Across two Europe PMC queries - one of which returned 22 records, every title screened - and six of the earlier worker's PubMed searches on the same topic, no record measured nerve damage in skin after an injected local anaesthetic by any design. The claim's attribution of the one skin measurement to lidocaine patches is verified from the Wehrfritz abstract, including the route, the healthy-volunteer population, the 42-day exposure and the direction of the effect. This is the same claim as W-M005 on the mepivacaine page, which another worker in this session holds; the two verdicts should be reconciled before either is written up. Kept to study design and existence throughout, with no thresholds or lethal values recorded.
_note: same claim as W-M005 on a different page

proposed_wording: No measurement of duration, injection pain or skin blood flow after an intradermal bupivacaine wheal in neuropathic leg skin was found in searches of Europe PMC and in the earlier worker's PubMed searches through October 2026; the figures available for this route come from healthy volunteers' forearm, lower-back and hand skin. Intracutaneous local-anaesthetic injection has been studied in neuropathic human skin at other body sites: a randomised trial of repetitive intracutaneous local anaesthetic with steroid in acute thoracic herpes zoster exists (Cui et al. 2017, PMID 27492741), with pain scores and postherpetic-neuralgia incidence as outcomes rather than block duration or blood flow.
reason: The claim is a provenance statement about the page's own figures and it holds: every source traced for those figures is a healthy-volunteer intradermal study, and two Europe PMC queries (29 records screened in full, and the top 100 of 241) plus six of the earlier worker's PubMed searches found no intradermal bupivacaine measurement in neuropathic leg skin. The claim is scoped to neuropathic leg skin, so healthy-volunteer studies narrow it at most, and nothing found narrows it: the closest records miss on population, intervention or outcome. Worth recording beside it, though, is that intracutaneous local anaesthetic has been given to neuropathic human skin elsewhere on the body with pain outcomes (PMID 27492741, PMID 29995761, PMID 16300701), so a broader 'nothing by this route in damaged skin' reading would be too strong. The bupivacaine page states its negatives flatly, so the sentence is judged as written.

The nearest design found is a randomised, double-blind trial in healthy volunteers that varied the injected volume at a fixed dose for an ultrasound-guided common peroneal nerve block and found no difference in mean sensory block duration (PMID 31789898); the route is a nerve block rather than a wheal, and the solutions differed in concentration rather than being the same solution. reason: Searches found nothing matching: three Europe PMC queries (11, 16 and 1 records, all screened) and two of the earlier worker's PubMed searches turned up no side-by-side timing of intradermal wheals differing only in volume. The studies that do vary volume against duration miss either the route (peripheral nerve block rather than an intradermal wheal) or the intervention (the solution's concentration changed with the volume), so they do not narrow a claim scoped to wheals of the same solution in skin. The page's own description of its estimate as an interpolation between two studies differing in tissue layer, endpoint and country is therefore accurate on this evidence.

records_read.citation: Howe NR, Williams JM. Pain of injection and duration of anesthesia for intradermal infiltration of lidocaine, bupivacaine, and etidocaine. J Dermatol Surg Oncol 1994;20(7):459-64
records_read.what_it_matches_or_misses: The trial the page cites. Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blinded, 20 subjects, intradermal, pH-matched; three agents only. Its abstract states that lidocaine hurt least and etidocaine hurt most, which verifies the claim's second half. Covers three of the seven agents, so it narrows the all-seven claim at most.

records_read.citation: Prien T. Intradermal anaesthesia: comparison of several compounds. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 1994;38(8):805-7
records_read.what_it_matches_or_misses: Randomised, double-blind, 600 patients; six preparations given as intradermal skin wheals - saline, prilocaine, lidocaine, two mepivacaine products and procaine - with infiltration pain rated on a visual analogue scale. Five local anaesthetic preparations of four distinct agents, so it covers at least three of the seven on the comparison page (lidocaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine) plus procaine, and so reaches more of them than the three-agent trial the page cites; but it includes neither bupivacaine nor ropivacaine nor articaine nor etidocaine and so does not cover all seven.

quote: To compare the efficacy of different local anaesthetics to produce intradermal anaesthesia for venous cannulation and the discomfort associated with skin infiltration.
proposed_wording: No intradermal injection-pain comparison covering all seven agents was found; a Europe PMC search requiring articaine, ropivacaine and bupivacaine together with injection-pain terms returned no records. The three-agent trial the page cites does report that etidocaine hurt most (Howe and Williams 1994, PMID 8034840). Larger intradermal infiltration-pain comparisons exist and are not cited on the page: a randomised, double-blind trial in 600 patients compared five local anaesthetic preparations of four agents - prilocaine, lidocaine, mepivacaine in two products, and procaine - as intradermal wheals for infiltration pain (Prien 1994, PMID 7887101), and a randomised, double-blind within-subject study in 20 volunteers rated discomfort on injection across six intradermal solutions (Wightman and Vaughan 1976, PMID 791022).
reason: The claim is scoped to all seven agents and nothing found matches that scope, so the headline negative stands: a Europe PMC query requiring articaine, ropivacaine and bupivacaine with injection-pain terms returned zero records, and the earlier worker's two PubMed injection-pain searches (88 and 141 records, both screened in full) found no seven-agent comparison either. The second half of the claim is verified from the cited trial's own abstract. What narrows the claim is the implication that only a three-agent comparison exists: Prien 1994 compared five local anaesthetic preparations of four agents intradermally for infiltration pain in 600 randomised patients, among them mepivacaine and prilocaine, and Wightman and Vaughan 1976 compared six intradermal solutions in 20 volunteers, so the page's 'what would settle it' sentence - which asks for mepivacaine and prilocaine to be included and says none exists - overstates the gap for part of that set. On which trial 'is cited for the claim': Howe and Williams 1994 (PMID 8034840) is the intradermal injection-pain trial that found etidocaine worse and is the better fit; Morgan 1975 (PMID 1138776) compares the same three agents and its full text is being read by another worker in this same session, so the attribution should be settled against that reading before the page is edited.
_note: the trial usually cited compared three agents and found etidocaine worse

records_read.citation: Yang S, Abrahams MS, Hurn PD, Grafe MR, Kirsch JR. Local anesthetic Schwann cell toxicity is time and concentration dependent. Reg Anesth Pain Med 2011;36(5):444-51
records_read.what_it_matches_or_misses: Matches every element. Schwann cells cultured from neonatal rat sciatic nerve were exposed to five local anaesthetics - lidocaine, mepivacaine, chloroprocaine, ropivacaine and bupivacaine - across four concentrations, and each was assessed for cell death after 4, 24, 48 and 72 hours of exposure. That is a time-course whose shortest point is hours rather than days, run for five drugs, and the abstract reports a result at brief exposure as well as at the long ones. Free full text in Europe PMC as PMC3380610.

quote: We sought to test the hypothesis that LAs are toxic to Schwann cells and that the degree of toxicity is directly related to the concentration of LA and duration of exposure.
proposed_wording: A time-course of local-anaesthetic exposure in Schwann cells exists and its shortest exposure is measured in hours: Schwann cells cultured from neonatal rat sciatic nerve were exposed to five local anaesthetics - lidocaine, mepivacaine, chloroprocaine, ropivacaine and bupivacaine - and assessed for cell death after 4, 24, 48 and 72 hours (Yang et al. 2011, PMID 21857272, free full text in Europe PMC as PMC3380610), and the paper reports a result at brief exposure as well as at the longer ones. What was not found is the same time-course run in skin, or at the exposure a wheal delivers in skin rather than in culture.
reason: A study matching every element exists, and it is the same paper the page is discussing. Yang 2011 ran the design the claim asks for - a time-course whose shortest exposure is hours - for five local anaesthetics, and reports an outcome at the brief exposure as well as at 24, 48 and 72 hours, so 'it has not been done for any drug' does not hold as written. The page itself records that this study read toxicity at 4, 24, 48 and 72 hours, so the sentence contradicts the page's own description of the source two sections earlier; the correction needed is to the wording. What survives the correction is narrower and still true: the time-course was run in cultured rat Schwann cells, not in skin, so it does not establish what an intradermal wheal delivers to Schwann cells in dermis. Recorded as design and existence only; no threshold figure is reported here.

proposed_wording: No study of repeated bupivacaine injection over months into skin that has already lost nerve fibres, with intraepidermal nerve fibre density or any other measure of skin change as the outcome, was found in searches of Europe PMC and in the earlier worker's PubMed searches through October 2026, and none was found for the other agents in this group. A full screen of the 22 Europe PMC records that combine an intraepidermal-nerve-fibre-density title term with any of these agents found none in which an injected local anaesthetic was the exposure. The nearest designs found are a randomised trial of repetitive intracutaneous local anaesthetic with steroid in acute thoracic herpes zoster over weeks, with pain outcomes and no measure of skin innervation (PMID 27492741), and repeat epidermal nerve fibre density measured over time in fibre-depleted distal leg skin with a non-drug exposure (PMID 26002840).
reason: Searches found nothing matching. Three Europe PMC queries - including one of 22 records whose every title was screened, and the top 100 of a 117-record query - plus four of the earlier worker's PubMed searches turned up no record in which repeated injected local anaesthetic was the exposure and a measure of skin innervation the outcome, in any population. The claim is scoped to skin that has already lost fibres, so healthy-volunteer and topical studies narrow it at most, and the one repeated-exposure study with an innervation outcome (PMID 21530339) is topical, in healthy skin, and over days rather than months. The claim's own extension to every drug in the group also holds on these searches. The outcome measure the page names is available and has been used longitudinally in fibre-depleted skin for other exposures, so the gap is the intervention rather than the method.

quote: Lidocaine hurt least and etidocaine hurt most.
proposed_wording: No published source reporting 40.5 mm as an injection-pain score for plain bupivacaine was found: a Europe PMC search for that phrase together with bupivacaine returned one record, an unrelated conference proceedings volume. The study usually credited with the figure, Howe and Williams 1994 (PMID 8034840), is subscription-only and is not held in Europe PMC or PubMed Central, and its abstract gives the injection-pain result as an ordering of the three agents rather than as numbers. The companion figure in circulation is traceable: a systematic review of local anaesthetics for digital nerve blocks reports 53 mm as the highest mean pain on injection and attributes it to bupivacaine with epinephrine, not to plain bupivacaine (Vinycomb and Sahhar 2014, PMID 24612831).
reason: All three parts of the claim hold. A phrase search for the figure together with bupivacaine returned a single, unrelated record; Howe and Williams 1994 is confirmed paywalled from its Europe PMC record, which carries only a subscription link and no PubMed Central copy; and its abstract reports the injection-pain comparison as an ordering, with the duration result given as percentages and no millimetre values anywhere. The page's attribution of the 53 mm figure to bupivacaine with epinephrine via the digital-nerve-block review is also verified from that review's abstract. A pain score is an outcome rather than a drug amount, so the figure is reported here rather than omitted. One caveat on the engine: Europe PMC's handling of a numeric phrase is loose - the same phrase searched without bupivacaine returned 567 records matching unrelated measurements - so absence from this engine is weaker evidence than a clean phrase index would give.
needs_full_text: Howe NR, Williams JM 1994, J Dermatol Surg Oncol 20(7):459-64, PMID 8034840 - full text, to establish whether 40.5 mm originates in its results tables or figures. Not needed for the verdict, which is about what was found, but it is the only way to settle the figure's provenance.
_note: a sourcing claim about a figure in circulation; the figure is a pain score in mm, not a drug amount
